taxonomyNote: NatureServe's primary common name is Common Mud Turtle and it keeps K. subrubrum (with subspecies) as one species; Reid et al. (2025) propose restoring the Mississippi mud turtle (K. hippocrepis) to species rank.
fieldMarks: Two plastral hinges under an oval carapace that is solid brown, olive with irregular yellow streaks, or solid black.
Head has irregular, often jagged markings or stripes between eye and nostril; limbs smudged grey, brown or black.
Tail tipped with a spine; notch at the rear of the plastron.
Males: longer tail, larger head, patch of raised scales on the hind legs.
Striped mud turtle (K. baurii) has a pair of head stripes and carapace stripes; K. subrubrum has no carapace stripes.
behavior: Solitary and largely crepuscular in summer; active year-round in the south, hibernates about November-March in the north.
Seldom basks; bottom feeder on insects, mollusks, crustaceans, amphibian larvae, carrion and aquatic plants.
In South Carolina spent late summer through winter about 170 days in upland refugia up to 135 m from wetlands.
habitat: Shallow, slow or nonflowing fresh or brackish water with soft bottom and abundant vegetation, and wet meadows; frequently travels overland.
Nests in soft soil in open areas not far from water.
range: Eastern United States from Long Island, New York south to the Florida Panhandle, west along the Gulf Coast to eastern Texas and north to southern Illinois and Indiana; disjunct population in northwestern Indiana.
